title: Physics
target_note: g = 10 N/kg throughout. About 90 seconds a question; two-step calculations are the norm.

questions.stem_html:
A polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth. The rod gains 5 × 1012 electrons. The charge on an electron is −1.6 × 10−19 C.

What is the charge on the cloth afterwards?
questions.solution_html: The cloth loses the electrons the rod gains, so it is left positive. Magnitude 5 × 1012 × 1.6 × 10−19 = 8 × 10−7 C. +8 × 10⁻⁷ C

traps.E: Charge is conserved overall, but it is separated: the cloth is not neutral.

questions.stem_html: A 12 V battery drives 3 C of charge through a lamp in 5 s. What is the power of the lamp?
questions.solution_html: E = QV = 36 J. P = E/t = 7.2 W. (Or I = 0.6 A, P = IV.)

traps.A: This is the current in amps.
traps.D: The energy in joules, not the power.
traps.E: Multiplied by t instead of dividing.

questions.stem_html:
The circuit shows a 12 V cell of negligible internal resistance, a 3 Ω resistor, and two 6 Ω resistors in parallel.

What is the power dissipated in one of the 6 Ω resistors?

questions.solution_html:
Parallel pair: 3 Ω. Total 6 Ω, so the main current is 2 A. Voltage across the pair = 2 × 3 = 6 V, so each 6 Ω resistor carries 1 A.

P = I2R = 1 × 6 = 6 W.

traps.B: Used V²/R with V = 6 V but R = 12 Ω.
traps.D: Used the full 2 A through one 6 Ω branch (I²R = 24) halved.
traps.E: Used 2 A through a 6 Ω resistor: the current splits.

questions.stem_html:
A filament lamp is rated 12 V, 24 W. When connected to a 6 V supply it draws 1.5 A.

What is the ratio (resistance at 12 V) : (resistance at 6 V)?
questions.solution_html: At 12 V: I = 2 A, R = 6 Ω. At 6 V: R = 6/1.5 = 4 Ω. Ratio 3 : 2. Resistance rises with temperature, as the V–I curve for a filament shows.

traps.D: Assumes ohmic behaviour; a filament is not.
traps.E: Guessed from 12 : 6.

questions.stem_html:
A fixed 2 kΩ resistor is in series with an NTC thermistor across a 6 V supply. At 20 °C the thermistor has resistance 4 kΩ; at 60 °C it has resistance 1 kΩ.

By how much does the voltage across the thermistor change when the temperature rises from 20 °C to 60 °C?
questions.solution_html: Voltage divides in proportion to resistance. At 20 °C: 6 × 4/6 = 4 V. At 60 °C: 6 × 1/3 = 2 V. Falls by 2 V.

traps.B: Arithmetic slip in the second divider.
traps.C: The supply is fixed but the share across the thermistor is not.
traps.D: Read the change across the fixed resistor with the wrong sign.
traps.E: This is the change across the fixed resistor (2 V to 4 V).

questions.stem_html:
A transformer is 100% efficient. The primary is connected to 230 V and the secondary supplies 11.5 V to a device drawing 4 A.

What is the current in the primary coil?
questions.solution_html: VpIp = VsIs: 230 × Ip = 11.5 × 4 = 46, so Ip = 0.2 A.

traps.E: Multiplied by the turns ratio instead of dividing.

questions.stem_html:
A power station transmits 1 MW along cables of total resistance 5 Ω. Initially it transmits at 10 kV. The transmission voltage is then raised to 100 kV, with the power transmitted unchanged.

By what factor is the power lost in the cables reduced?
questions.solution_html: Current = P/V: 100 A then 10 A. Loss = I2R: 50 kW then 500 W. Factor 100. Ten times the voltage, a tenth the current, a hundredth the loss.

traps.A: The cable resistance, irrelevant to the ratio.
traps.B: The current ratio; loss goes as the square.
traps.E: Cubed the ratio.

questions.stem_html:
A straight wire at right angles to a uniform magnetic field experiences a force of 0.3 N. The field strength is doubled, the current is halved and the length of wire in the field is tripled.

What is the new force?
questions.solution_html: F = BIL: factor 2 × ½ × 3 = 3. 0.9 N.

questions.stem_html:
An ac generator produces a voltage with peak value 6 V and period 40 ms. The coil is then rotated at twice the speed.

What are the new peak voltage and period?
questions.solution_html: Faster rotation cuts field lines faster, doubling the induced voltage, and halves the time per cycle. 12 V, 20 ms.

traps.A: Forgot that the rate of cutting flux (and so the voltage) also doubles.
traps.D: Doubled the period instead of halving it.
traps.E: Inverted both.

questions.solution_html: Distance = area: ½ × 4 × 12 + 6 × 12 + ½ × 2 × 12 = 24 + 72 + 12 = 108 m. Average speed = 108/12 = 9 m s⁻¹.

traps.E: The peak velocity, not the average.

questions.stem_html: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 20 m s−1. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s−2, at what height above the launch point is its speed 10 m s−1?
questions.solution_html: v2 − u2 = 2as: 100 − 400 = 2(−10)s, so s = 15 m.

traps.B: Halved the max height (20 m) by assuming linear energy.
traps.D: The maximum height, where the speed is zero.
traps.E: Sign error: 100 + 400 = 2 × 10 × s gives 25, then a slip.

questions.stem_html:
A 4 kg block and a 6 kg block are connected by a light string on a smooth horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 30 N pulls the 6 kg block, so the string pulls the 4 kg block along behind it.

What is the tension in the string?
questions.solution_html: Whole system: a = 30/10 = 3 m s−2. The string is the only horizontal force on the 4 kg block: T = 4 × 3 = 12 N.

traps.C: 6 × 3, the net force on the 6 kg block, not the tension.
traps.E: Assumed the tension equals the pull.

questions.stem_html:
A 2 kg trolley moving at 6 m s−1 collides with a stationary 4 kg trolley and they move off together.

How much kinetic energy is lost in the collision?
questions.solution_html: Momentum: 12 = 6v, v = 2 m s−1. KE before = ½ × 2 × 36 = 36 J; after = ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 J. Lost 24 J.

traps.B: The final KE, not the loss.
traps.E: The initial KE; momentum is conserved, KE is not, but not all of it is lost.

questions.stem_html:
A 0.05 kg ball hits a wall at 20 m s−1 and rebounds along the same line at 15 m s−1. The contact lasts 0.01 s.

What is the average force on the ball?
questions.solution_html: Velocity changes from +20 to −15, a change of 35 m s−1. Δp = 0.05 × 35 = 1.75 kg m s−1. F = 1.75/0.01 = 175 N.

traps.A: Used the change in speed 5 m s⁻¹.

questions.detail: Force as rate of change of momentum

questions.stem_html: A spring of stiffness 200 N m−1 obeys Hooke's law throughout. It is already extended by 0.1 m. How much additional work is needed to extend it to 0.3 m?
questions.solution_html: E = ½kx2: at 0.1 m, 1 J; at 0.3 m, 9 J. Additional work 8 J.

traps.B: ½ × 200 × 0.2² treats the 0.2 m increase as if from zero.
traps.D: Assumed energy is linear in extension.
traps.E: The total energy at 0.3 m, forgetting the 1 J already stored.

questions.stem_html: A 2 kg object is dropped from rest at a height of 20 m and hits the ground at 15 m s−1. How much energy is transferred to the surroundings by air resistance during the fall?
questions.solution_html: GPE lost = 2 × 10 × 20 = 400 J. KE gained = ½ × 2 × 225 = 225 J. Difference 175 J.

traps.B: Used v = 20 m s⁻¹ for a 200 J KE.
traps.E: The GPE, not the loss.

questions.stem_html: A crane lifts a 500 kg load through 12 m in 20 s. The crane motor is 60% efficient. What is the electrical input power to the motor?
questions.solution_html: Useful energy = 500 × 10 × 12 = 60 kJ. Useful power = 3 kW. Input = 3/0.6 = 5 kW.

traps.E: Forgot the 20 s, then halved.

questions.stem_html: A skydiver is falling at terminal velocity and then opens the parachute. Which statement is correct for the instant just after the parachute opens?

options.A: The skydiver moves upwards because drag exceeds weight.
options.B: The skydiver decelerates because drag exceeds weight.
options.C: The skydiver's velocity is unchanged because drag equals weight.
options.D: The skydiver accelerates downwards because weight exceeds drag.
options.E: The skydiver decelerates because weight has decreased.

questions.solution_html: Opening the parachute suddenly increases drag while the speed is still high, so drag > weight: resultant force upwards, so the downward velocity decreases. The skydiver keeps moving downwards, just more slowly, until a new lower terminal velocity is reached. B

traps.A: An upward resultant force does not mean upward motion; velocity is still downward.
traps.C: Drag equalled weight before the parachute opened, not after.
traps.D: That describes the start of the fall, not the parachute opening.
traps.E: Weight does not change.

questions.stem_html: A 2 kW kettle heats 0.5 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J kg−1 °C−1. Assuming all the energy goes into the water, how long does this take?
questions.solution_html: E = 0.5 × 4200 × 80 = 168 000 J. t = 168 000/2000 = 84 s.

traps.B: A mass of 0.125 kg was used.
traps.E: Used a 1 kW kettle.

questions.stem_html:
0.2 kg of ice at 0 °C is turned into water at 20 °C. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 340 000 J kg−1; specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J kg−1 °C−1.

How much energy is required?
questions.solution_html: Melting: 0.2 × 340 000 = 68 000 J. Warming: 0.2 × 4200 × 20 = 16 800 J. Total 84 800 J.

traps.E: Warmed the water through 100 °C.

questions.stem_html:
An air bubble of volume 2 cm3 is released at a depth of 20 m in a lake. Atmospheric pressure is 100 kPa, the density of water is 1000 kg m−3 and g = 10 N kg−1. The temperature is constant.

What is the volume of the bubble just before it reaches the surface?
questions.solution_html: Pressure at 20 m = 100 kPa + hρg = 100 + 200 = 300 kPa. PV constant: 300 × 2 = 100 × V, V = 6 cm³.

questions.stem_html: 200 cm3 of liquid A (density 0.8 g cm−3) is mixed with 300 cm3 of liquid B (density 1.2 g cm−3). The volumes simply add. What is the density of the mixture?
questions.solution_html: Mass = 160 + 360 = 520 g. Volume = 500 cm3. Density = 1.04 g cm⁻³.

questions.stem_html: A solid cuboid measures 0.5 m × 0.2 m × 0.1 m and is made of material of density 2000 kg m−3. What is the greatest pressure it can exert when resting on one face on a horizontal floor?
questions.solution_html: Volume 0.01 m3, mass 20 kg, weight 200 N. Smallest face 0.2 × 0.1 = 0.02 m2. Pressure = 200/0.02 = 10 kPa.

traps.C: Used 200/0.04, a face that does not exist.
traps.E: Doubled the weight.

questions.stem_html: A person claps and hears the echo from a wall 0.5 s later. The speed of sound is 340 m s−1. A sound of frequency 1700 Hz is then produced. How many wavelengths of this sound fit between the person and the wall?
questions.solution_html: Distance to wall = 340 × 0.5/2 = 85 m (the sound goes there and back). Wavelength = 340/1700 = 0.2 m. 85/0.2 = 425.

traps.D: Forgot to halve the round-trip distance.

questions.stem_html: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters glass, where its wavelength becomes 400 nm. The speed of light in air is 3 × 108 m s−1. What is the speed of light in the glass?
questions.solution_html: Frequency is unchanged at a boundary, so v ∝ λ: 3 × 108 × 400/600 = 2 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

traps.D: Assumed speed is unchanged; it is frequency that stays the same.
traps.E: Inverted the ratio; light slows down in glass.

questions.stem_html:
A nucleus of bismuth-212 (atomic number 83) emits an alpha particle, and the product then emits a beta-minus particle.

What are the mass number and atomic number of the final nucleus?
questions.solution_html: Alpha: mass −4, atomic −2 → 208, 81. Beta-minus: mass unchanged, atomic +1 → 208, 82.

traps.C: Alpha decay applied to the atomic number with the wrong sign.
traps.D: Mass number changed by 2 instead of 4.
traps.E: Beta applied to the mass number.

questions.stem_html: The activity of a sample falls from 800 Bq to 100 Bq in 36 minutes. How long after the start does the activity first reach 25 Bq?
questions.solution_html: 800 → 100 is three halvings in 36 min, so the half-life is 12 min. 100 → 25 is two more halvings: 24 min. Total from the start: 36 + 24 = 60 min.
